title: People, Not Passwords, Why You Need a Catchphrase or Two to Define Your Challenges This Fall ur-challenges-this-fall
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Prompted by a former student's offhand question — "will you be teaching students or usernames this fall?" — Dave Stuart Jr. argues that a well-chosen catchphrase can help teachers and teams stay oriented to their humanizing goals during distance learning. Drawing on Dan Coyle's research into high-performing cultures in The Culture Code, he explains that effective catchphrases work because they're "navigational," compressing a group's central strategy into language that's fast to say and easy to remember. Stuart lands on "people, not passwords" as his own catchphrase for the fall, then demonstrates how to use it in context rather than as an empty slogan, modeling sample staff-room lines that tie the phrase to specific commitments around humanizing online spaces and protecting teacher work-life balance. He closes with several bonus quotes from Coyle's book on trust and team performance.
points: Effective catchphrases work when they're "navigational" — compressing a team's central strategy or values into an easy-to-repeat shorthand, per Dan Coyle's research.
Stuart's chosen catchphrase, "people, not passwords," is meant to keep humanizing relationships at the center of distance-learning decisions.
He warns that picking a catchphrase is the easy part; the real work is repeatedly filling it with specific meaning tied to concrete strategies, not just repeating it as a slogan.
The piece models catchphrase use in realistic staff-room dialogue, showing how the same phrase can anchor conversations about both student relationships and teacher work-life balance.
quotes: So, Mr. Stuart, will you be teaching students or usernames this fall?

Coyle's insight is that catchphrases work when they are navigational — when they form a shorthand way of speaking to a group's central aims (Coyle calls these "North Star" phrases), central strategies, or central values.
But it doesn't stop at picking — that's just the easy part. The hard part is making sure to fill the catchphrase up with lots of meaning.

A lot of our students are going to initially feel like the online learning space is cold or daunting or detached from their life. Here's what we're going to do to humanize our online learning spaces from Day 1.
There is such a thing as too much pressure, and I'm sensing that a lot of us are on the wrong side of Yerkes-Dodson. People over passwords — we're people too!
Vulnerability doesn't come after trust — it precedes it. Leaping into the unknown, when done alongside others, causes the solid ground of trust to materialize beneath our feet.
